title: The first truth, in full
hookLine: birth, aging, sickness, death, sorrow, not getting what you want: this is dukkha (SN 56.11)

lines: EVERYONE ELSE HAS IT FIGURED OUT.
cards: Late at night, a quiet thought can slip in: everyone else seems to have this figured out. Their parents aren't getting old. Their bodies don't ache.

They didn't just lose someone, or miss out on the thing they wanted. Scroll long enough and the feeling hardens into a fact. In a deer park outside Varanasi, the Buddha's first sermon answered that thought with a list.
Not a list of your problems. A list of everyone's.

teach.b: The sermon is the Turning of the Wheel of the Dhamma, number eleven in the fifty-sixth book of the Connected Discourses. Five former companions are listening. After the middle way, the Buddha names the first truth.
In Rhys Davids's old translation it begins: "Birth is attended with pain, decay is painful, disease is painful, death is painful."
The list keeps going: being joined to what you dislike is painful, being parted from what you love is painful, and not getting what you want is painful.
In some versions of the teaching, sorrow, lament, grief and despair are named too.

Then a summary line: in short, the five heaps that make up a person, body, feeling, perception, mental formations and consciousness, when they're clung to, are dukkha. Look at what's on the list. Nothing exotic.
Nothing that happens only to the unlucky, or the unwise, or people who did something wrong. Birth, aging, getting sick and dying happen to kings and to beggars.
Not getting what you want happens to everyone, every day, usually before lunch. The Buddha isn't diagnosing you.
He's diagnosing being human. And the word he uses, dukkha, has been rendered many ways in English: pain, suffering, ill, unsatisfactoriness, stress.
It's a wide word, covering the funeral and the stubbed toe and the long wait in a hospital corridor. The list says: all of this is real, and none of it means you're failing.

how: In Theravada communities the first sermon is often chanted on Asalha Puja, the full moon that tradition says marks it, and the first truth's list is chanted in Pali.

o: a punishment for something you did wrong
the pain and unease every human life meets
the belief that life is only misery

games.q: match the pieces of the first truth.
p: the Turning of the Wheel of the Dhamma
the five heaps, clung to, are dukkha

s: the first truth lists troubles that come only to people who've done wrong
birth, aging, sickness and death come to everyone; the list is general.
not getting what you want is on the list
the first sermon names it right after being parted from what you love.
translators all agree dukkha means suffering
it's been rendered pain, suffering, ill, unsatisfactoriness and stress: it's a wide word.

games.q: you're one of the five in the deer park. the Buddha has just named birth, aging, sickness and death. what does he name next?
o: being parted from what you love, and not getting what you want.
games.why: he widens the list to ordinary heartbreak and frustration, then sums it up: the five heaps, when clung to, are dukkha.

practice: Let your day so far replay at an easy speed, and each time you find a small sting, a late bus, a sore back, a message that didn't come, name it quietly: dukkha, with no commentary and no blame.
Once or twice, let the thought widen: somewhere, right now, someone else has this exact one.

wordCard.voice: Dukkha. Pain, suffering, unsatisfactoriness: birth, aging, sickness, death, and not getting what you want, belonging to everyone, not a sign that you're failing.

orig.note: Pali dukkha: pain, suffering, unsatisfactoriness; a word wide enough for grief and for a stubbed toe.

carryVoice: Your line: it's not just you. The list belongs to kings and beggars alike. Day three hundred thirty-four, done.
